note: Standard German forms a Swiss German writer replaces: ist (isch), nicht (nöd, nid,
ned), ein/eine (en, e), auch (au), kann (cha), muss (muess), hat (hät, het), gibt
(git), kommt (chunnt), etwas (öppis), gewesen (gsi), schon (scho), von (vo), auf (uf),
aus (us), bei (bi), Schweiz (Schwiiz), and infinitives in -en where dialect drops the
n. Left out because Swiss German texts use them as well: das, dass, die, der, des, es,
sind, wird, nur, noch, zu, vom, wo, mit, und, dafür, erste, einfach (written Swiss
German keeps this spelling beside eifach); sein is left out for French au sein de.
English function words. Left out because another of the six languages writes them too:
was, will, also, so, man, war, an, am, in (German), on, me, correct, but (French but,
'aim'), no (Italian), be (Romansh be, 'only'), were (Swiss German were, 'become'), do
(Swiss German do, 'there'), or (the German abbreviation OR of the code of
obligations), has (Romansh ti has, 'you have'), as (Swiss German as, 'than', and
Romansh sch'as).
is stays, though some Swiss German answers write is for isch.
French function words and verb forms. Left out: au (Swiss German au, 'also'), des
(Swiss German des, 'that'), du and je (German du, je nach), le, ne and ce (Italian),
qui (Italian 'here'), mais (Romansh mais, 'months'), dis (Romansh dis, 'days'), en
(Romansh en, 'in'), ans (Romansh ans, 'us', and German ans), plus and exact
(English), Suisse (in names such as Tox Info Suisse that every language uses), il, la,
sa, l', d', n', c', s' (shared with Italian or Romansh). sur stays, though Romansh has
it for 'over'.
Italian articulated prepositions (della, nel, sulla), verb forms and adverbs where
Rumantsch Grischun writes otherwise: non (na ... betg), questo (quest), anche (er,
era), più (pli), con (cun), o (u), anni (onns), Svizzera (Svizra), vero (vair), così
(uschia). Left out because Rumantsch Grischun writes them too: il, la, al, da, dal,
per, che, è, ed, ma, senza, questa, quella, prima, sa, hai, po, and di (Romansh di,
'day'). Left out for other collisions: alle (German alle), nei (Swiss German nei,
'no'), ci (French celle-ci), ai (an English abbreviation). non stays, though French
writes it and English uses it as a prefix (non-EU): in a French or English text it
is one vote against many. o stays, though the Engadin idioms write it for 'or'.
